author: Erich Reimer
title: Amid reports from Nikkei that Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) is expec
text:
Amid reports from Nikkei that Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) is expected to downgrade its iPhone X guidance on Thursday significantly for Q1 2018 amid disappointing sales, nonetheless Apple still looks like it will be gaining ground thanks to hopefully having gained valuable consumer insights from this cycle as well as benefiting from the recent corporate tax reduction.
The iPhone X was a major risk due the dramatic changes in design and functionality, as well as price. However as smartphones increasingly trend toward higher-capacity computing capabilities and software hosting, Apple will be a step ahead of the game thanks to having jumped ahead early on and studying the consumer market for such products.

(Source: Apple)
With Earnings On Thursday, A Monday Bombshell From Nikkei Nikkei broke the news on Monday that Apple is expected to downgrade its iPhone X guidance and production for the upcoming quarter, as weaker-than-expected holiday sales seem to mean that the iPhone X just didn't catch on as much as all the hype for it had hoped.
Based on conversations with those familiar with the matter, Nikkei states that Apple will downgrade Q1 2018 iPhone X production from 40 million to just 20 million, a 50% production cut. Apple is expected to keep iPhone 8 and 8 Plus production steady at 30 million.
Apple stock did not react well to the news. After already being in a downtrend in the lead-up to earnings, the stock fell even further in the wake of the reports.
AAPL Price data by YCharts In terms of analyst reactions, Sanford C. Bernstein & Co. Analyst Toni Sacconaghi estimates that Apple's Q1 2018 phone shipments will be down 20% year-on-year from 66 million to 53 million, with the average price per phone rising over 17% year-on-year to $767.
While Sacconaghi still believes the stock is overall on a positive path, he also slashed FY18 estimates from 247 million to 220 million, meaning just 1.3% annual growth in units shipped.

(Figure: Global Apple iPhone Unit Sales, Source: Statista)
Walter Piecyk of BTIG maintains that despite the downgrade he still is bullish and has a price target of $198 due to Apple's continued demonstrated growth despite its size combined with tax reform tailwinds.
Deustche Bank's Sherri Scribner took the news to mean that Apple might not necessarily be seeing a super cycle in 2018, as the iPhone X's price for function just wasn't enough to drive massive sales.
Reports for the past several weeks have already indicated that consumers have had significant problems with the iPhone X ranging from its price to functionality, such as claiming it's too fragile and easy to break .
However all is not lost for Apple. The company clearly still sold a lot of these high-priced iPhone Xs, as well as iPhone 8s and other products, that still will likely result in a decent quarter, even if perhaps not the one that the iPhone X super-hype had led many to believe it would have.
Furthermore, as I've previously discussed , the iPhone X never seemed to really be about just driving sales and adoption for this particular model. The iPhone X wasn't just a new iPhone release like most previous ones, but rather an almost completely new product that consumers simply have had little exposure to in the past.
The iPhone X's main feature upgrades were its OLED ("organic light-emitting diode," which also was the primary driver behind the increase in production cost per smartphone) screen, high capacity bionic chip processing that allowed it to do functions such as facial recognition, lack of a headphone jack, and missing home button.
These features are likely ones that many smartphones in the future will feature as graphics and computing chip processing capabilities increase significantly along with the growth of software applications and functions that utilize that computing potential.
Yet in this initial roll out Apple seemed to be dragged by the high production cost for the iPhone X due to Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) being the only supplier capable of manufacturing enough OLED chips, the design difficulties that led to reports of fragility, the discarding of popular functions, and thus overall resulting in consumers not willing to pay the high price to adopt it at the moment.
However Apple undoubtedly will learn from this episode, study consumer data closely, and in the future better modify its supply chain, design, and consumer marketing to be able to better adapt to this still-rapidly expanding market ahead of its smartphone peers. And when it does, that will indeed allow Apple to see even greater growth at its already massive-size.

(Source: 9to5Mac)
In the meantime, it looks like Apple has many other pro-growth prospects on the horizon as has announced it will be investing over $350 billion in the United States over the next five years, in part due to the lower corporate income tax rates from the recent D.C. tax reform bill.
The funds will vary, but appear like they will be spent on projects ranging from a new campus to data centers to manufacturing. With the reduction of tax barriers and rates, Apple will undoubtedly gain significantly from being able to better navigate and play in the U.S. market.
Furthermore, with some iPhone X variants seemingly still planned this year that have everything ranging from larger screens to lower costs, perhaps those will sell well where the original iPhone X couldn't.
Conclusion Though it appears that the iPhone X may not be the great rainmaker it was originally hoped to be, nonetheless Apple is still likely to benefit well from having entered boldly into the new smartphone market this early.
With the firsthand consumer and market information gained from the iPhone X's cycle Apple will likely be able to better design its future manufacturing process, product design, and sales strategy to better maximize consumer adoption.
Given the seemingly improved versions of the iPhone X already coming out this year it looks like Apple will soon enough be able to put that knowledge to use almost immediately.
Despite the iPhone X hype perhaps having been too much, Apple still looks like it's still finding ways to continue to gain ground despite its already massive size.
